description: We are a multidisciplinary team skilled in AI/Deep Learning, research, data analysis, and web development. We aim to use NASA data and modern technology to solve real-world problems through innovative, research-driven solutions. We welcome members with skills in AI/ML, GIS, UI/UX, space science, and data visualization
summary:
Picture a flame aboard the International Space Station: no rising smoke, no flickering tip, just a dim blue sphere that can keep burning almost unseen. That is the fire astronauts must face, and FIREWISE-X was built to help them understand it.

Grounded in NASA’s PSI-25 BASS-II experiments (129 ISS flight runs, 52 videos), FIREWISE-X opens on a Mission Control dashboard. In the Flame Analysis Studio, real orbital footage plays beside an AI segmentation overlay as faint flames are traced, measured, and tracked frame by frame. The Pre-Mission Assessment lets engineers dial in oxygen, airflow, and fuel thickness, then shows what really happened in the closest flight experiments, with warnings at the edge of tested limits and side-by-side scenarios. The Astronaut Assistant answers in plain language, cites the exact NASA page, and refuses to guess. Research Reports turn any run into evidence cards and a one-click PDF, while the Validation Suite openly shows where the system succeeds and fails.

As crews travel toward the Moon and Mars, help from Earth grows distant. FIREWISE-X turns NASA’s flight science into evidence they can trust, supporting every human decision and never replacing it.
details:
FIREWISE-X: Flame in Freefall
AI-assisted microgravity fire intelligence, built on NASA’s PSI-25 BASS-II flight experiments

The problem: fire that breaks the rules

On Earth, a flame is easy to read. Hot gas rises, fresh air rushes in, and the flame stands tall and bright. In orbit, buoyancy almost disappears. A flame becomes a dim, blue, slowly creeping sphere, sometimes nearly invisible to the eye. Cutting off airflow can leave it smoldering quietly for many seconds, then it flares back to life when ventilation returns. Instincts trained on Earth can mislead even an experienced crew.

NASA has already flown the experiments that show this behavior. The Burning and Suppression of Solids-II (BASS-II) investigation burned solid fuels inside the International Space Station’s Microgravity Science Glovebox across 129 flight runs and 52 videos. FIREWISE-X takes that flight science out of the archive and puts it in the hands of the people who plan missions and fly them.

What it does and how it works

FIREWISE-X is a web platform with six connected modules:

1. Mission Control Overview. Users land on a cinematic dashboard: a microgravity flame over deep navy, real dataset counts, recent analyses, and one-click routes into every tool. It shows real backend statistics, never simulated telemetry.

2. Flame Analysis Studio. Real ISS footage plays side by side with an AI segmentation overlay. Our computer-vision pipeline uses two filters: one catches the bright yellow-orange soot core, the other catches the faint blue outer flame that the eye can barely see. Telemetry text burned into the old flight video is masked out so it isn’t counted as flame. Frame by frame, the Studio measures flame area, growth rate, front speed, and centroid motion, plotted on a timeline. Users can step ±1 or ±5 frames, inspect any moment, and export the results to JSON.

3. Pre-Mission Assessment. An engineer sets oxygen concentration, airflow speed, and fuel thickness. Instead of a guess from a black-box model, FIREWISE-X searches all 129 flight runs and returns the closest real experiments, ranked by a normalized, weighted physical distance. It reports what actually happened in those runs: sustained burning, radiative quenching, or blowoff. If an input moves outside the flight-tested range, a clear warning appears. Scenarios A, B, and C can be compared side by side, so planners can see how one change, such as lower oxygen or stronger airflow, shifts the outcome.

4. Astronaut Assistant. This is a domain-specific microgravity fire-safety assistant, not a generic chatbot. Every answer cites the exact page of NASA’s BASS-II technical report. Questions its evidence doesn’t cover get a plain refusal: “I do not have verified flight data on that inquiry in the BASS-II archive.” Crew or ground controllers can enter sensor readings and compare them against reference flight runs, and the assistant keeps sensor deviations clearly separate from confirmed fire events.

5. Research Reports. A searchable, paginated archive of every experiment. Each run has a seven-part Evidence Card: observation, rule triggered, flight conditions, source citation, supported hypothesis, limitations, and recommended next step. One click generates a 9-section PDF report, from experiment metadata through video analysis, run matching, scenarios, limitations, and references.

6. Validation Suite. The platform tests itself in the open. On a 15-frame hand-annotated benchmark, segmentation reached 87.4% mean IoU. Leave-one-run-out cross-validation across all 129 runs matched 68.2% of outcomes exactly, rising to 84.6% inside the tested range. Known failure cases and refusal cases are listed openly, so every judge, researcher, and user can see where the system is strong and where it isn’t.

Benefits

  • Safer planning before launch: engineers can explore fire behavior under different cabin conditions, anchored to real flight results.
  • Answers you can verify: every output traces back to a specific NASA run or report page.
  • Honest about uncertainty: the platform shows its limits, its weak spots near extinction boundaries, and what it doesn’t know.
  • NASA data made accessible: users never dig through raw folders, and the original NASA files are kept unchanged.
  • Works anywhere: it runs fully offline on a local workstation, and in the cloud with static fallbacks if the backend goes down.

Intended impact

Artemis, the Gateway, and future Mars transits will carry crews farther from Earth than ever, with longer communication delays and less real-time support from mission control. Fire in a sealed spacecraft is one of the most serious dangers a crew can face. FIREWISE-X shows that past NASA flight experiments can become living, evidence-based guidance: for engineers choosing materials and ventilation settings before launch, and for crews trying to understand what they are seeing during flight. It is also a learning tool that lets students and researchers explore microgravity combustion through real flight data. It is a research prototype, built to strengthen human judgment and approved NASA procedures, never to replace them.

Tools, languages, hardware, and software

  • Languages: Python 3.10+, TypeScript
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Recharts, Lucide React
  • Backend: FastAPI, NumPy, OpenCV (color-space segmentation, morphological filtering, kinematics), ReportLab (PDF generation)
  • Data: NASA Physical Science Informatics PSI-25 BASS-II dataset and the NASA/TM-20210011385 final report
  • Deployment: Vercel in the cloud, with pre-rendered JSON fallbacks, plus a one-click local launcher for offline use
  • Hardware: standard laptops only; the vision pipeline runs on CPU at about 14 ms per frame, with no GPU needed

How it is creative

Our boldest decision was to not trust a black box. With 129 flight runs, a neural network would confidently predict conditions it had never seen, and in a spacecraft that is dangerous. So we built an engine that answers a more honest question: “What actually happened in the closest real flight experiments?” We then tested it as rigorously as any trained model, holding out each run one at a time.

Other creative elements:

  • Seeing the nearly invisible: two-filter segmentation tuned for dim, blue, sooty microgravity flames that standard fire detectors miss.
  • Masking burned-in video text: a fix for legacy ISS footage, where telemetry text printed over the video would otherwise be counted as flame.
  • An assistant that knows when to say no: refusal is a deliberate safety feature.
  • Evidence Cards: every scientific claim comes with its source, its limits, and a next step.
  • Validation inside the product: our weaknesses are on display, not hidden in a footnote.

Factors our team considered

  • Life-critical safety: no invented measurements, and the system never activates suppression or overrides the crew.
  • Extrapolation risk: explicit warnings whenever inputs leave the flight-tested ranges of oxygen, airflow, and thickness.
  • Scientific integrity: original NASA files kept unchanged, data provenance tracked, and validation split by experiment to prevent data leakage.
  • Data alignment: we didn’t assume videos, sensor records, and table entries line up. Labels show which data are discrete chamber measurements and which are continuous video.
  • Honest language: we banned hype terms like “zero hallucination” and “flight validated” and report exact numbers instead.
  • Human oversight: any real flight use would need independent validation, approved hardware, and mission infrastructure.
  • Usability and access: a clean, calm interface, responsive design from 320 px phones to 4K screens, and offline operation for spacecraft settings.
